stats.label: net cash, after a Lawns to Legumes grant

principles.d: Kill turf with cardboard and mulch rather than stripping sod. Less work, and no soil disturbance to wake up weed seeds.
Plugs at 12–18 in. spacing close in by year 2–3, which crowds out weeds.
Start where beds already exist, so each phase looks finished on its own.
A 12–18 in. strip of lawn along the sidewalk and driveway frames the plantings and signals “this is on purpose.”

deadlines.title: Lawns to Legumes
deadlines.detail: Spring 2027 cycle, up to $400 back on native plants and seed. About 30 minutes online. Apply in the property owner's name.

deadlines.title: Rochester Garden Grant
deadlines.detail: Up to $1,000 (25% match) for 2027 pollinator and runoff work. Contact the coordinator for a site visit first. Not for the boulevard.

z1.t: Open front lawn (already mostly bee lawn)
z1.body:
The lawn is already clover-rich. The gap is early spring, before the clover gets going.

  • Frost-seed white clover and self-heal into thin spots in late Feb–Mar: scatter on frozen ground and let freeze-thaw work it in
  • Add early bloomers that tolerate mowing: native violets and wild strawberry, plus crocus bulbs (non-native, well-behaved) planted this fall
  • Mow at 3–4 in., 2–4 times a year, and hold the first mow until the early bloomers finish
  • No fertilizer or broadleaf herbicide: both knock back clover

corner.body:
Grows the existing inside-corner bed out along the south side of the front wing. A short-to-mid prairie mix, 1–3 ft tall: prairie dropseed, little bluestem, anise hyssop, wild bergamot, purple coneflower, rough blazing star and aromatic aster.

About 150 plugs at 15–18 in. spacing.

fdn.body:
With T1 gone, this corner gets afternoon sun. Widen the foundation bed about 8 ft west to wrap the stump in low sun natives: wild strawberry, pussytoes, nodding onion, harebell and little bluestem, with columbine at the edge.

Keep healthy shrubs and swap tired ones for bush honeysuckle (Diervilla lonicera) or New Jersey tea.

Existing bed contents and the exact stump spot are unverified.

shade.body:
The spot where turf grows worst (shade from T4, T5 and the fence) becomes a woodland-edge planting: Pennsylvania sedge as the groundcover, with wild geranium, zigzag goldenrod, big-leaved aster and wild ginger, plus 2–3 native shrubs.

A 3 ft mulch path runs along the house to the backyard fence. Remove the old beehive first.

border.light: Part sun (6 ft fence to the south)
border.body:
A prairie border along the neighbor's privacy fence, linking the corner bed to the sidewalk. Leave a 2 ft mown or mulched strip at the fence so they can maintain it.

The fence shades it from the south, especially in spring and fall, so favor part-sun species: wild bergamot, golden alexanders, zigzag goldenrod and prairie dropseed.

Seeding instead of plugs saves about $200 but takes 2–3 years to fill in.

blvd.light: Part shade north half (T2), part sun south
blvd.body:
Option A, bee lawn: extend the front lawn's bee lawn to the boulevard. It's still mown turf, so very likely no permit is needed. Confirm with Forestry that clover and thyme count as turf.

Option B, native strip: needs the free Natural Landscape Permit. Keep plants 18 in. from the curb and sidewalk, which leaves a ~4 ft core, and plan on staying under ~24 in., lowest by the driveway apron.

  • Don't prune T2 or T3: only licensed companies may, with a permit
  • Call 811 before digging
  • Expect plow snow and road salt

blvdB.body: The plantable core after 18 in. setbacks from the curb and the sidewalk. Short, salt-tolerant natives. A city permit is required, and no hardscape until Forestry approves it.

path.body: 3 ft wide, shredded mulch over cardboard. Runs along the house to the backyard fence, through the spot where the old beehive sits now. Gate location to verify.

stump.body:
Make it the centerpiece of a small island instead of working around it. Pick one:

  • Bee bath: a shallow saucer of pebbles on top, kept topped up. Pollinators need shallow water with landing spots
  • Rot it faster: drill a grid of 1 in. holes, pack them with compost or clippings, and bury it under the Phase 1 mulch

Either way it becomes habitat: rotting wood feeds beetles and fungi, and cavity-nesting bees reuse old beetle tunnels. Clip root suckers, and top up the dip with free topsoil as the roots decay. Skip a bee hotel here: ground-level wood stays damp. Mount one 3–6 ft up on a sunny wall instead.

rain.body:
A barrel at the front downspout by the wing's southwest corner (location to verify). An inch of rain on just 100 sq ft of roof is about 62 gallons, so the overflow matters more than the barrel.

Run overflow at least 10 ft from the foundation into a shallow dip planted with swamp milkweed, blue vervain, great blue lobelia and fox sedge. Ornamentals only, keep it covered against mosquitoes, and drain it before the first hard freeze.

hive.body: If it's a managed honey bee hive, have a local beekeeper check it before it's moved. Old comb can carry American foulbrood spores, and robber bees from other hives carry them home. Close the entrance until then, then remove the hive or hand the equipment over. Its spot becomes part of the shade bed and path.

house.body: Split-entry. The garage faces the street at the north end, and the front door sits just south of it, up a short stoop. The lawn slopes gently down from the house to the sidewalk.

drive.body: Keep boulevard plantings low near the apron so you can see when backing out.

north.area: ~3 ft wide (mapped line may be off)
north.body: A narrow strip between the house and the north line. The mapped line looks too close to the house, which suggests an offset. Measure before planning anything here.

back.body: Behind the backyard fence. Not part of this plan.

T2.body:
Fine-textured leaves in Street View (possibly an elm or hackberry). Its canopy shades the north half of the boulevard and the lawn by the drive.

Species are guesses from photos. Don't till or cut sod inside the drip line; smother and hand-plant instead.

T3.body:
Compound leaves in Street View (honeylocust or Kentucky coffeetree look). It overhangs the lot's southwest corner.

Species are guesses from photos. Don't till or cut sod inside the drip line.

T4.body: A ~20 ft tree in front of the south end of the house, near the backyard fence. It anchors the shade bed, and its species decides how shady Z4 really is.

T5.body: A tall tree on the far side of the fence. It shades the south strip from the south.

plants.note: Rusty-orange winter color; host for skipper butterflies
One of the last flowers of the year
The native one, not the invasive bush honeysuckles
The groundcover that replaces turf in shade
Flowers hide under the leaves; grown for the groundcover
Fills the late-spring gap before the prairie wakes up
Host for fritillary butterflies; tolerates mowing
Not native, but the backbone of a bee lawn
Optional; first forage of the year

timeline.d: Apply to Lawns to Legumes (by Nov 30) and contact the Rochester Garden Grant coordinator for a site visit (closes Dec 31). Both go in the property owner's name. Awards come in January, and only purchases after the award notice are reimbursed, so hold off on plants until then.

Before the ground freezes: mark the Z2 extension (~165 sq ft) and the stump island (~100 sq ft). Scalp-mow, lay cardboard with 6 in. overlaps and the tape removed, soak it, and cover with ~4 in. of free city mulch (~3.3 cu yd). 2–3 people, half a day. If it goes quickly, smother Z4 too (~6 cu yd). Optional: plant ~100 crocus in the lawn.

Tape-measure and photograph the front. Settle the plant list and order plugs for May pickup. Choose boulevard Option A or B. In late Feb or March, frost-seed white clover and self-heal into thin lawn spots: scatter on frozen ground and let freeze-thaw work it in (~30 minutes).
Call 811 a few days ahead. Cut X-slits in the cardboard and plant ~210 plugs at 15–18 in. spacing. Swap the foundation shrubs and set up the stump. Water 2–3 times a week for the first month.

timeline.t: Smother Z4 and the south border
timeline.d: Cardboard and mulch again (if Z4 wasn't done in fall). Remove the old beehive first. Both areas are plantable by September.

timeline.when: Weekend 4 · late Aug to early Sep 2027
timeline.d: Mow the boulevard to ~2 in. and rough up the soil with a rake; rent an aerator only if it's compacted. Seed ~265 sq ft at ~5 lb per 1,000 sq ft, topdress lightly, and keep it moist for 3–4 weeks. Spot-seed thin patches in the front lawn the same day.
~200 plugs and 2–3 shrubs, plus the mulch path. Fold into Weekend 4 if you'd rather keep it to six weekends.
Smother the boulevard strip and apply for the Natural Landscape Permit, with a site plan and maintenance plan.
~115 plugs in the border, plus the boulevard strip if it's permitted.
Leave stems standing over winter, since many native bees nest in them. Cut back in late spring once it's consistently warm. Weed 2–3 times a summer and mow the bee lawn 2–4 times a year.

programs.offer: Up to $400 reimbursed for native plants and seed
programs.fit: Apply by Nov 30, 2026 for the Spring 2027 cycle. Buy only after the January award notice.

programs.offer: Up to $1,000 reimbursed (25% match) for pollinator and water-stewardship gardens, including up to $200 of equipment rental
programs.fit: Strong fit for Phases 1–2. Apply Oct 1–Dec 31 for 2027 installs. Not in the right-of-way. Strings: 5-year maintenance agreement, a city sign, open for public viewing, and hosting a “garden party.”

programs.offer: 90% of cost, up to $100, one barrel per address
programs.fit: Currently limited to Cascade Creek pilot neighborhoods (Kutzky, Washington, Lowertown), so this yard likely isn't eligible yet.

programs.offer: Free for a donation; the county compost site suggests $20 per pickup load
programs.fit: Makes smothering essentially free. ~14 cu yd over two years. Check free material for jumping worms.

private.t: State law protects managed natural landscapes
private.d: Minn. Stat. 412.925 (2023) requires every city to allow a planned, intentional, maintained planting, which may exceed 8 in. and go to seed. An unmown lawn left to go wild doesn't count.

private.t: No permit needed on private land
private.d: Rochester amended its Tall Grass and Weeds ordinance (Code 8-5) in July 2024 to match. Turf grass over 12 in. still needs a permit anywhere.
The state law binds cities, not homeowners associations. A 2025 Plymouth lawsuit put that gap on display. Check any covenants before Phase 1.

boulevard.d: The abutting owner mows it and keeps it weed-free. The city owns and cares for the trees.
Plain lawn, or likely a mown bee lawn, is allowed as is. Confirm with Forestry that clover, thyme and self-heal count as turf.

boulevard.t: Anything else: free Natural Landscape Permit
boulevard.d: Needs a site plan, plant list and succession, and a maintenance plan.
Keep all vegetation 18 in. back from sidewalks and the street. That leaves a ~4 ft plantable core here.
Trim to the sidewalk edge, 8 ft above sidewalks and 14 ft above the street. Pick plants that don't flop.
Only licensed tree companies get permits to work on boulevard trees. Don't prune T2 or T3; hand-dig gently in their root zones. A second boulevard tree almost certainly won't be approved.
No height cap for permitted plantings and no rules on edging, rocks or raised beds. Ask Forestry. Until then: plants under ~24 in., lowest by the driveway, no hardscape.
Boulevards often carry buried utilities. Gopher State One Call is free and required by state law.

openQuestions.t: Is there an HOA or recorded covenant covering landscaping?
Confirm species for T2–T5, and what the T1 stump was (some species sucker from the roots).
Old beehive: managed honey bee hive? Is there a local beekeeper who can check it?
What's in the existing beds (Z2, Z3), and what's worth keeping?
Sun check: photos of the front at ~10 am, 1 pm and 5 pm on a sunny day, once leaves are out.
Ground-level photos from each front corner and of the boulevard.
Tape-measure the house setback, bed edges and boulevard width.
Drainage: soggy spots? Water sheeting off the driveway? Is the lawn fertilized or treated with weed killer now?
Boulevard: Option A (bee lawn) or Option B (permitted native strip)?
Look and feel: tidy and formal, or meadowy? Any must-have or banned plants?
Is the city mulch shredded wood or wood chips? Shredded wood is what the Garden Grant reimburses.
